title: Where the pass-through money goes: money in, money out, what was kept
question: The agencies that receive the largest child-care sums pay most of it on. Does money in equal money out plus what was kept, and who receives it?
finding: In fiscal 2025 the City paid Children's Council of San Francisco $113.5 million (or $149.2 million, counting $35.7 million that the City's file labels fiscal 2025 although its voucher numbers and dates fall in June 2024) and the State promised it up to $35.9 million; its tax return shows $209.7 million of government money received, $186.8 million paid onward (89% of spending), $17.6 million in pay and benefits and $6.3 million in other costs, so the return balances to a surplus of $2.1 million. Onward payments rose from $96.8 million in 2021. The grants schedule names no onward recipient: the whole sum is reported as grants to individuals in 4 lines ("Child care Subsidies and Child care Provider Stipends": 2,547 recipients, $100.6 million; "Quality Grants": 119 recipients, $31.9 million; "ECE Workforce Compensation Enhancements": 2,551 recipients, $52.4 million; "Nutrition": 222 recipients, $1.9 million; ECE on the return stands for early care and education). The same is true of Wu Yee Children's Services ($49.4 million paid onward in 2025). The only providers either return names are its five highest-paid contractors (next screen); the Low Income Investment Fund names its recipients (the screen after). The City's own nonprofit-spending dataset shows $4.4 million to Children's Council for the same year, because it leaves out the two largest agreements. Its City agreements on file list 172 objectives, and no published result against them was found.
how: City paid is every payment to the agency in the City's voucher table made in the fiscal year that ends with the tax year (July to June); the year a payment was made is read from its voucher number, not from the fiscal-year label printed on the line. State promised is the sum of State contract maximums for that year (published from 2022-23). The rest is from each agency's Form 990: government grants received, grants paid out and how they are classified, pay and benefits, other costs, management costs and surplus. Kept share is everything not paid out as grants, as a share of spending. The gap column is government grants on the return minus City payments and State maximums. The dataset column is what the City's Citywide Nonprofit Spending dataset shows for the same agency and year, as that dataset labels the year.
limits: An agency of this kind is large because of the families it pays for, not because of what it spends on itself; the kept share is the figure that describes the agency. A return that balances shows only that the agency's own books add up. The returns report payments to child-care providers as grants to individuals, a part of the form that asks for a kind of grant, a number of recipients and a total, not names; so the providers, among them private centres and family homes, cannot be checked from the grants schedule. Two other files in this project are built on the City's nonprofit-spending dataset and therefore show far smaller City payments to these agencies than the voucher table does (the last two columns link to them). The gap between the return and the two public payment files can be State amendments made after the first allocation, federal meal money, money for work in other counties, and timing. The Low Income Investment Fund works nationwide, so most of its figures are not San Francisco money. The record that would answer who was paid is each agency's provider payment ledger, which the City receives under its agreements. The payment file labels each line with a fiscal year that is not always the year the payment was issued: some earlier payments, mostly on purchase orders in multi-year capital funds, are filed under a later year, and the Controller's own published figures follow that label. Payments are dated here by voucher number, a single running sequence, which moves $5.52 billion of $119.3 billion (4.6%) to an earlier year than its label; $1.08 billion of that belongs to fiscal 2018 or earlier, before the file starts. Near the turn of a year the number dates a payment to within a few days. Read from the label instead, the voucher table shows $149.2 million paid to Children's Council in fiscal 2025 and $114.0 million in fiscal 2024, against $113.5 million and $149.7 million here. The difference in fiscal 2025 is 8 payment lines worth $35.7 million that carry the label 2025 and voucher numbers from fiscal 2024; the file's own date column puts them between 17 June 2024 and 18 June 2024, 12 days before fiscal 2024 ended. A payment issued in June for the year that starts in July would look like this, and the label may be the year the City charged it to; the Controller's own published figures for nonprofits follow the label.
